mcqs.question: A file system uses contiguous allocation. Why might it fail to grow an existing file even when the disk has plenty of total free space?
options: Contiguous allocation caps every file at exactly one block
The block immediately after the file's current run might already belong to another file, and free space elsewhere is scattered, not adjacent
Growing a file always requires reformatting the disk
Contiguous allocation cannot support files larger than 1MB
mcqs.explanation: Contiguous allocation needs the extension to be the very next block; if that block is taken, growing in place fails even though other free blocks exist elsewhere on disk — external fragmentation, not a hard size or single-block limit.

mcqs.question: In pure linked allocation, what does the directory entry for a file actually store?
options: Pointers to every block of the file
Only the address of the first block; every other block is found by following pointers
A bitmap of all blocks used by the file
The total file size only, with block locations computed mathematically
mcqs.explanation: Linked allocation stores just the starting block in the directory entry; each block then points to the next, so all other blocks are discovered by walking the chain rather than being listed anywhere centrally.

mcqs.question: How does a FAT-style file allocation table improve on pure linked allocation without switching to indexed allocation?
options: It eliminates the need to know the file's starting block
It converts random access into true O(1) lookups
It moves the next-block pointers into a table that can be cached in RAM, avoiding a disk read per chain hop
It removes the possibility of a broken pointer chain entirely
mcqs.explanation: FAT keeps the chain-following model but relocates pointers into an in-memory table, so walking the chain costs RAM lookups instead of disk reads per hop. It's still O(n) in the chain length, and a corrupted table entry can still break the chain.

mcqs.question: Unix inodes keep a handful of direct block pointers plus single/double/triple-indirect pointers, rather than a uniform multilevel index for every file. Why?
options: Most files are small, so most files never need indirection at all — only large files pay the extra lookup cost
Direct pointers are required by the SSD hardware controller
Indirect pointers are illegal in the POSIX file system standard
It's purely historical and has no performance benefit today
mcqs.explanation: The combined scheme optimizes for the common case: small files resolve in one hop via direct pointers, and only the rare large file walks one, two, or three levels of indirection. It's a deliberate, still-relevant performance trade-off, not a hardware or standards requirement.

mcqs.question: Which allocation method gives O(1) random access to any block AND avoids external fragmentation?
options: Contiguous allocation
Linked allocation
Neither — you must always trade one for the other
Indexed allocation, via a per-file index block of pointers
mcqs.explanation: Indexed allocation gets both: an index block gives direct O(1) lookup to any data block, and because data blocks don't need to be adjacent, there's no external fragmentation. Contiguous has fast access but fragments; linked avoids fragmentation but is O(n) to seek.
